title: Australia's Film Industry Boom: How a Tax Break Lured Hollywood Down Under
summary:
If you build it, they will come. That's the story of Australia's film industry after the government increased the Location Offset—a tax incentive for international productions—from 16.5% to 30% in July 2024. The result has been a dramatic surge in film and TV production, with spending reaching a record $1.93 billion in the 2024/25 financial year, according to Screen Australia. That's a 14% increase from the previous year.

Local productions also saw a huge boost, with expenditure up 76% to $270 million, including several films with budgets over $35 million. International studios are flocking to Australia. Producer Bennett Walsh, currently working on "The Big Fix" starring Mark Wahlberg and Riz Ahmed, says, "The Location Offset is what is anchoring the industry. Since then both Amazon and Netflix have started to come here. Amazon is on its 12th project." Walsh has shot multiple films in Australia, including "Mortal Kombat II" and "Subversion."

Kate Marks, CEO of Ausfilm, notes the trend of repeat business: "We are seeing studios coming back—Amazon, MGM, Netflix, Legendary, Sony, Warner Bros., and Disney—but we are also seeing talent returning." Disney Studios Australia in Sydney hosted a high-profile slate including Legendary's "Street Fighter" and Netflix's "Apex." The pace has accelerated into 2026, with an Apple Original feature occupying eight of nine soundstages.

Productions are also spreading beyond traditional hubs like Melbourne and Sydney. The Jake Gyllenhaal and Kevin Costner film "Honeymoon With Harry" is shooting in Brisbane, and the first U.K.-produced TV shows are filming in new Perth studios. Western Australia has tripled production size in three years.

Animation is thriving too, boosted by the success of "Bluey." Laura DiMaio of Princess Bento says, "With a huge show like 'Bluey' introducing people to our Australian humor, we've unlocked a new audience." Flying Bark, the studio behind Netflix's "Stranger Things: Tales from '85," is working on a "Zak Power" movie and a "Ghostbusters" TV adaptation. Australian animators are "punching above their weight," says Barbara Stephen, CEO of Flying Bark.

With generous incentives and a growing reputation for creativity, Australia's film industry shows no signs of slowing down.
why_it_matters: Australia's film boom shows how a single government policy can reshape an entire industry, creating thousands of jobs and putting more diverse stories on screens worldwide. For young people, it means more pathways into creative careers — from animation to visual effects — without having to leave the country.

background_read: Screen Australia (the Australian government's key film and TV funding body) and Ausfilm (an agency responsible for attracting international production to Australia) have long pushed for competitive tax incentives to lure big-budget projects.

Around the world, countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, and Ireland have used similar rebates to become major filmmaking hubs. Australia's jump from a 16.5% to a 30% Location Offset made it one of the most attractive destinations overnight.

Before this surge, Australian film production had peaks and valleys, often dependent on the value of the Australian dollar and government policy changes. The record $1.93 billion spending reflects a massive injection of cash into the local economy, creating thousands of jobs for crews, builders, caterers, and visual effects artists.

The success of local animation, particularly the global phenomenon 'Bluey,' has also proved that Australian stories and humor can find massive audiences abroad, encouraging studios to invest in more original content down under.

perspectives.description: The surge in production brings billions of dollars into the Australian economy, supporting local businesses and employment. It also elevates Australian talent and stories on a global stage, giving homegrown directors, writers, and animators a platform they might not have had otherwise.

Overdependence on Hollywood blockbusters could make the industry vulnerable if incentives are reduced or another country offers a better deal. Some worry that local, original Australian voices might get squeezed out by big-budget international productions taking up studio space and crew resources.

Australia's policy mirrors a worldwide trend where nations compete to attract filmmaking by offering ever-larger rebates. This creates a race to the bottom where governments might give away more than they gain, but for now, Australia's 30% rate has positioned it as a top-tier destination without being the absolute highest globally.

To keep the boom going, Australia will need to invest in training local workers and building permanent infrastructure, not just temporary stages. AI and virtual production technologies could change the equation — Australia might need to adapt its incentives to cover those areas, while maintaining the human storytelling edge that brought hits like 'Bluey' to screens.
